ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 7 MAP
Renaissance Art
Semester 2 · 3 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
When art turns its full attention to the human being, what changes?

This unit opens Semester 2 with the Renaissance, the rebirth of classical antiquity in Italy around 1400. You will study humanism and the lifelike portrait in Leonardo, the geometry of deep space in Raphael's perspective, and the idealized human body in Michelangelo's sculpture and fresco. The unit's theme is the rebirth of the human.

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 8 MAP
Baroque & Rococo
Semester 2 · 3 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
How does art use drama, light, and spectacle to move us, and to serve power?

Around 1600 the calm balance of the Renaissance gave way to drama. This unit explores the Baroque, an art of movement, deep shadow, and intense emotion: Caravaggio's spotlight of light and meaning, Bernini's marble caught mid-motion, and Versailles, where grandeur became royal power. It ends with the Rococo, the lighter, playful style that followed. The theme throughout is Drama, Light, and Spectacle.

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 9 MAP
Neoclassicism, Romanticism & Realism
Semester 2 · 3 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
When art turns from reason to passion to plain truth, what does each choice say about what matters in life?

This unit follows three movements that argued with one another. Neoclassicism revived the order and civic virtue of ancient Rome for an age of reason and revolution. Romanticism rebelled with emotion, the power of nature, and the sublime. Realism then turned to plain, honest truth, painting ordinary working people with the dignity once reserved for kings. Together they open the modern era. The module theme is Reason, Passion, and Real Life.

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 10 MAP
Impressionism & Post-Impressionism
Semester 2 · 2 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
When painters trusted their own eye over the rules of the studio, what new things could a painting be?

In the 1870s the Impressionists carried their easels outdoors to capture the fleeting moment of light with bright color and quick, broken brushwork. A generation later the Post-Impressionists kept that color but pushed past the passing moment toward order, structure, and feeling: Seurat’s pointillism, Cézanne’s search for the geometry under nature, van Gogh’s expressive color. Together they open the door to modern art.

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 11 MAP
Modern & Contemporary Art
Semester 2 · 3 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
When art stops copying the world, what is it doing instead, and who gets to decide what counts as art?

This is the final unit of the course. In the early 1900s, artists broke the centuries-old rule that a painting must be a window onto the visible world. Cubism shattered the single viewpoint; abstraction left the object behind; Surrealism painted the dream; Abstract Expressionism poured out pure feeling; Pop Art turned to mass culture; and contemporary art keeps asking what art can even be. Carry your four-step analysis skills into works that look nothing like where the year began.

How you will view the art this unit. Some works here are still under copyright, so the course does not reproduce them; for those, each lesson links you to the official museum page. Teacher Guide — Semester 2 Culminating Project: Art Historian Portfolio

Art History & Criticism 1 Honors (0100330)

Teacher-facing only. No benchmark codes, answer keys, or tier labels on student pages.

What it is

The year-end capstone. Students assemble a curated portfolio of their strongest work from across both semesters (analysis, comparison, and creation pieces) plus a final reflective essay tracing how their eye, judgment, and writing grew. Major project, 100 points (the Map weights Major Projects & Assessments at 60% of the grade). Follows the AHC Map: "Art Historian Portfolio including analysis assignments, comparison assignments, selected creative activities, and a final reflection."

Files

  • cp2-00-art-historian-portfolio-guide.html — interactive Project Guide (Tier 4 scaffolding, GitHub-deployed): what an art historian's portfolio is, selecting work across both semesters, organizing the Word document (with a generic table-of-contents visual), and writing the final reflection, plus optional VR gallery. Engine: reflect + select.
  • CP2-01-art-historian-portfolio-assignment.html — Canvas-native graded assignment (Tier 3, 100 points): six required components, full M365 Word Skill Step (Table of Contents / Styles), 4-criterion rubric, citation requirement, optional VR enrichment.

Tier / load

This is the cycle's single Tier-3 teacher-graded assessment and the largest grading event of the year. Rubric is 4 criteria, consistent in spirit with the course's other rubrics. Budget about 10 to 12 min/student given the compiled length; most included pieces were already graded earlier, so focus fresh reading on the selection logic and the final reflection.

Standards alignment

VA.912.F.1.5 (digital presentation analyzing/comparing artists and works in historical context) is the anchor; also F.2.8 (exhibit/preserve art), F.3.5 (cited sources), C.1.4, H.1.4, C.3.5 (cross-cultural/timeline connections), and ELA.K12.EE.1.1 / EE.5.1 (evidence; format conventions). The reflective-essay component maps to the portfolio/reflection strand of VA.912.F. and to ELA EE codes for evidence-based writing. VA.912.C.1.3, added 2026-07-13: the reflection prompt now explicitly requires two criteria the student uses to judge their own work, learned from studied exemplars, with one of their own pieces measured against them; this is the course's named C.1.3 assessment (the creation activities' artist's-note self-assessments build toward it all year). When grading the Reflection criterion, look for the two named criteria tied to real pieces. Texas (TEKS §117.302):* the portfolio anchors 4(C) and 4(D).

Deliverable & M365

Compiled Word document (.docx), Band C: title page, automatic Table of Contents via heading styles, page numbers, embedded photos of the student's own work, named LastName_FirstName_ArtHistorianPortfolio_AHC1H, saved to the course OneDrive folder, submitted via the Canvas OneDrive tab. Micro-cert moment: Insert a Table of Contents / Manage Styles (Word).

Notes

  • Copyright: students include only PD/CC images or photos of their own work; modern and contemporary works are linked to their official museum or foundation pages, never reproduced. This carries forward the Unit 11 link-out rule into the portfolio.
  • Required range: at least two analyses (from both semesters), at least one comparison/discussion piece, at least one creation piece, plus the reflection. Reward variety of era and kind of art.
  • The reflection is the graded heart: it must be the student's own honest, specific account of growth, tied to actual pieces. The assignment's AI callout makes clear AI cannot supply this.
  • The Unit 11 outro survey (Q5) seeds this project by asking which assignment each student is proudest of.
  • The optional VR gallery is platform-agnostic (place images and own creations on a wall, add labels, capture a walkthrough); it does not replace the Word portfolio.
  • Naming uses the CP2/cp2 prefix to mirror the Semester 1 CP1 capstone files.

Module 7.04 Quiz answer key (10 Q, 20 pts)

  1. B (rebirth)
  2. A (renewed focus on human beings, reason, dignity)
  3. A (sfumato)
  4. B (single vanishing point)

  7. C (ancient Greek sculptors)
  8. A (paints pigment into fresh, wet plaster)

  10. Matching: Mona Lisa → Leonardo / sfumato; School of Athens → Raphael / one-point perspective; David → Michelangelo / idealized form in marble; Sistine Chapel Ceiling → Michelangelo / fresco.

DAIJ model notes (for grading the T3 analysis)

Students choose Mona Lisa or School of Athens. A strong paper ties each step to visible evidence and uses unit vocabulary correctly. - Mona Lisa. Describe: seated woman, folded hands, faint smile, hazy landscape. Analyze: sfumato softens eye/mouth edges; pyramid pose gives balance; aerial haze deepens space. Interpret: humanism, an ordinary individual treated with the attention once reserved for saints. Judge: succeeds because the elusive expression still reads as living presence. Look for the words humanism, naturalism, sfumato. - School of Athens. Describe: crowd of philosophers in a vaulted hall, two central figures, receding arches. Analyze: linear perspective; orthogonals converge on a vanishing point between the central figures; deepest space frames the most important thinkers. Interpret: the geometry argues that the structure of the room mirrors the structure of knowledge. Judge: succeeds as a High Renaissance fusion of method and meaning. Look for linear perspective, vanishing point, orthogonals. - Common miss: describing the subject's biography/story instead of reading visible features. Push students back to what is literally on the surface in Describe and Analyze.

Engine rotation (per build conventions)

  • 7.01: flip (4 ideas) + select (2 rows). DAIJ Spotlight = Mona Lisa.
  • 7.02: select (2 rows) + flip (4 terms). Includes the one-point perspective concept SVG. DAIJ Spotlight = School of Athens.
  • 7.03: reflect (Unit 4 callback) + flip (4 terms) + select (2 rows). DAIJ Spotlight = David.
  • Every widget (each flip group, each select group, the reflect) carries its own Reset. Correct-answer indices are varied across widgets (7.01 select: c, b; 7.02 select: b, c; 7.03 select: c, a).

One-Point Perspective Drawing is a construction rung: the student builds a correct drawing from the perspective system taught in 7.02 (horizon line, vanishing point, orthogonals). Signature + portfolio save required. File: LastName_FirstName_PerspectiveDrawing_AHC1H.

assignments.title: Module 7.02 Assessment/Critique: Renaissance Masterpiece Analysis
assignments.html:
ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 7 · ASSESSMENT/CRITIQUE
Renaissance Masterpiece Analysis
Points: 40  ·  Submit: one Word document (.docx)  ·  Due: Week 2

Choose one work and write a full four-step analysis: Leonardo's Mona Lisa (shown below) or Raphael's School of Athens (from Lesson 7.02). Use the Renaissance vocabulary from this unit: humanism, naturalism, sfumato, linear perspective, vanishing point, idealized form.

Mona Lisa, Leonardo da Vinci, 1503–1507. Louvre, Paris. Public domain. (For the other option, use Raphael's School of Athens from Lesson 7.02 and the module Artwork Image Bank.)
📝 WRITE ONE PARAGRAPH PER STEP
D · Describe. What do you see? For the Mona Lisa, name the pose, hands, expression, and landscape; for the School of Athens, the hall, the central figures, the architecture. Only what is literally there.

A · Analyze. Explain how the work creates its effect: for the Mona Lisa, sfumato and the pyramid pose; for the School of Athens, how linear perspective and the vanishing point organize the space.

I · Interpret. What humanist idea about the human being does the work express? Tie every claim to your Describe or Analyze.

J · Judge. Does it succeed at expressing that idea, and how do you know? Build your verdict on the evidence above.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Write in Microsoft Word (Microsoft 365). Name your file LastName_FirstName_RenaissanceAnalysis_AHC1H, save it to your Optima › Art › ArtHistory_2026-27 OneDrive folder, and submit through the Canvas OneDrive tab. Target length: about one page (300 to 450 words).
M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Insert a Citation for an image (Word), so your chosen work is credited under the image.
⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · THE LOOKING IS THE ASSIGNMENT
An AI summary can list facts about the Mona Lisa or the School of Athens, but it cannot do your looking. The whole point of this analysis is to connect a specific feature you can see (a soft edge, a converging line) to the meaning it creates. Write from the work in front of you, in your own words, and tie each judgment to evidence you can point to.
✅ HOW YOU WILL BE GRADED (40 points)
CriterionPoints
Describe: accurate, specific, only what is visible10
Analyze: explains how the work creates its effect10
Interpret: humanist meaning tied to visual evidence10
Judge and vocabulary: reasoned verdict, correct terms10

assignments.title: Module 7.03 Studio Project: One-Point Perspective Drawing
assignments.html:
ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · MODULE 7 · STUDIO PROJECT
One-Point Perspective Drawing
Points: 20 (completion + effort)  ·  Submit: a photo (JPG/PNG) and a 2 to 3 sentence note

Renaissance artists turned a flat surface into deep space with one geometric rule. Now you will use that same rule yourself. This is a construction exercise: you build a correct one-point perspective drawing from the system you learned in Lesson 7.02, not from guesswork.

✏️ YOUR TASK
Your subject can be anything you like: a room interior, a city street, a hallway, a train track, a garden path, a bridge, whatever you want to send back into deep space. Color & Light Study
Points: 20 (completion + effort)  ·  Submit: a photo (JPG/PNG) and a 2 to 3 sentence note

The Impressionists and Post-Impressionists taught us to look at light and color before we look at objects. You will make a small study of your own. This is a variation exercise: you take the real methods you studied this unit and apply them to a scene you observe yourself.

✏️ YOUR TASK

discussions.title: Module 7.01 Discussion: How Art Saw the Human
discussions.html:
In Unit 6 you studied medieval art: flat, often gold-ground figures meant to point beyond the earthly toward the sacred. In Unit 7 you have seen Renaissance art turn toward the human being: lifelike faces, deep space, and the idealized body.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the medieval and Renaissance views of the human being on at least two points (for example: flat sacred figures vs. naturalistic individuals, gold ground vs. linear perspective, the soul's destination vs. the dignity of the living person). Name one specific work from each period as evidence. Then take a position: did the Renaissance reject the medieval view of the human, or extend it in a new direction?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of a medieval or a Renaissance work.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, one specific work from each period, a clear position, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Module 8.01 Discussion: Calm Ideal or Charged Moment
discussions.html:
Renaissance art prized calm, balance, and ideal beauty. Baroque art prized drama, movement, and intense emotion. Two artists can tell the same story very differently.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the Renaissance and the Baroque on at least two points (for example: Michelangelo's calm, still David vs. Bernini's twisting David caught mid-throw; or the even, balanced light of a Raphael vs. Caravaggio's single shaft piercing the dark). For each, say what feeling the style was reaching for. Then take a position: which approach do you find more powerful, and why? Support your view with specific works from Units 7 and 8.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast or similarity, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of a Renaissance or Baroque work.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position, specific works cited, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Module 9.01 Discussion: Romanticism vs. Realism
discussions.html:
Romanticism and Realism both rejected the cool order of Neoclassicism, but they pulled in opposite directions. Romanticism reached for heightened emotion, the power of nature, and the sublime. Realism reached for plain, unflattering honesty about ordinary life.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the two movements on at least two points (for example: epic drama vs. plain treatment; the storm-tossed individual vs. the anonymous worker; intense color and diagonals vs. muted color and a flat setting). Cite a specific work from this unit for each. Then take a position: which movement gives the truer picture of human life, and why?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast or similarity, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of The Raft of the Medusa or The Stone Breakers.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position, specific works cited, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Module 10.01 Discussion: Academic Art vs. Impressionism
discussions.html:
In the 1870s the official French Salon prized large, polished paintings finished smoothly in the studio, with crisp edges, careful detail, and serious subjects (history, myth, important people). The Impressionists offered the opposite: loose, quick, outdoor paintings of ordinary modern life that left brushstrokes visible and edges soft. Critics called the new work unfinished; the public was divided.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the polished academic style and the Impressionist style on at least two points (for example: finished detail vs. visible brushwork, grand subjects vs. ordinary life, studio control vs. outdoor light). For each, say what that approach was reaching for. Then take a position: was the “unfinished” Impressionist look a loss of skill, or a different and valid goal? Support your view with a specific work from this unit.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of a Monet, Renoir, or Cassatt.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position, a specific work cited, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Module 11.01 Discussion: Modern vs. Contemporary Art
discussions.html:
The early modern movements (Cubism, abstraction, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism) mostly stayed within painting and pursued a new way of seeing or feeling. Pop Art and the contemporary art that followed widened the field, drawing on mass culture and expanding into installation, new media, identity, and global voices, and asking outright "what is art?"

A reminder: link any work you discuss to its official museum page rather than reproducing the image.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare a modern movement with Pop Art or a contemporary approach on at least two points (for example: private feeling vs. public mass culture; paint on canvas vs. installation or new media; a single style vs. many styles and global voices). For each, name a specific work or artist and link it. Then take a position: did art improve, lose something, or simply change when it widened past the canvas?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast or similarity, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of a work either of you named.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position, specific works named and linked, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, no links, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.
